newsitem.title: NORWAY: Nobel Peace Prize winner is anybody's guess.
newsitem.headline: Nobel Peace Prize winner is anybody's guess.

text.p: Richard Holbrooke, the American architect of Bosnia's peace treaty, and former U.S. President Jimmy Carter are among the best known of 120 nominees for this year's Nobel Peace Prize, to be announced on Friday.

Other candidates mentioned by Norwegian news media include jailed Chinese dissident Wei Jingsheng, East Timor human rights champion Carlos Belo, Russian human rights campaigner Sergei Kovalyov and Leyla Zana, jailed Kurdish members of the Turkish parliament.
If the Nobel Committee decides to reward an organisation, the Salvation Army or medical aid charity Medecins sans Frontieres could win, Nobel watchers suggest.
But efforts to predict the secretive committee's thinking are, at best, only educated guesses.
In keeping with tradition going back to 1901, the five-member committee has revealed neither its shortlist nor even the names of nominees, who have only been identified by their own backers.

Nobel Institute Director Geir Lundestad revealed last week the committee had indeed reached a decision. "We cannot have giant surprises like we had last year but we will see," he said enigmatically. "I don't want to say anything more."
Nobel watchers were caught on the hop last year when the award went to little-known veteran anti-nuclear campaigner Joseph Rotblat and his Pugwash organisation.
Giving the $1.12 million prize to Carter, who has been nominated at least five times before, would come as no surprise.
Carter, who was president from 1977 to 1981, is recognised worldwide for his peacemaking and humanitarian efforts in Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and former Yugoslavia.

While other leading candidates have been nominated before, Holbrooke is a new name on the list of would-be peace laureates. He almost single-handedly brokered the 1995 Dayton peace treaty for war-torn Bosnia.
"Holbrooke is one of the hot names this year," Norway's TV2 television said on the late night news on Thursday. "Another strong candidate is...Carter."

China's Wei, regarded as the founder of the Communist state's tiny and embattled democracy movement, came to the fore last February when the Nobel Committee shrugged off a Chinese condemnation of him. The committee said it would not give in to pressure in selecting laureates.
Any hopes among Chinese dissidents of a revival of their beleaguered movement may lie with the Nobel Committee and whether it decides to select Wei.
However, few in China expect Wei, serving the first year of a 14-year jail term, to win the prestigious prize and thus halt the slow fading of Chinese dissent.
In China, members of Wei's family said they did not consider him a serious contender because of the strength of competition from front runners such as Holbrooke and Carter.

Friday's announcement of the peace prize, the only one of the Nobels to be made in Oslo, will conclude this year's batch of awards. The Nobel science, medicine, economics and literature awards have been announced in Stockholm in the past eight days.
